newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - EU Commission faces uphill task in financial area.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - EU Commission faces uphill task in financial area.

text.p: The European Commission has set itself the task of unblocking some of its most ambitious and controversial plans in the financial area.

According to Commission and industry sources, the EU executive is also mulling over whether to change bank reporting rules to reflect better the risks incurred in dealing with derivative products such as options and futures.
Originally meant to protect against market fluctuations, such instruments are now seen as a potential source of financial instability due to massive speculation.

The Commission's legislative work in the financial area is aimed ultimately at creating a truly European Union-wide market for banks, insurance companies and funds to go with a border-free, 370 million-strong Union.
But although the European single market is already a reality in the banking and insurance sectors, funds are still waiting for freer days.

At issue primarily is a long-standing proposal to allow for the $1.1-trillion European pension funds to be invested and managed freely throughout the EU. The Commission also has proposed to update legislation on investment funds to bring in new, more sophisticated, instruments such as money-market and cash funds.
Both draft directives have been deadlocked since 1994 at EU ministerial level with the result that most EU states still impose severe restrictions on the way funds are invested and managed.

Financial Services Commissioner Mario Monti wants to fight such restrictions, but EU officials stress progress is likely to remain slow. The restrictions range from the obligation to invest part of a fund's assets in local bonds to limitations on investment in foreign shares.
In a move to spur the momentum again on pension funds, the Commission is expected to adopt a green paper at the end of October which will address existing barriers as well as taxation problems.

More importantly, the discussion will also focus on whether there is any need for European-wide regulation of pension funds -- a point so far defended strongly only by the Commission and a few countries led by Britain.

Monti's staff are also hoping to revive the proposal to widen the scope of 1985 legislation on investment funds -- called the directive on Undertakings for the Collective Investment in Transferable Securities or UCITS -- to include cash and money-market funds as well as funds of funds.

But EU sources said that consultation with national governments had so far brought limited input and only highlighted the huge gap between the supporters -- the Commission and a Britain-led minority -- and the opponents of more freedom for funds.
Britain has the largest fund industry in the 15-nation EU.
The financial industry will also be eagerly waiting for the Commission's ideas on disclosure of derivatives and on new means of payments such as electronic money.

Derivatives disclosure became a very hot topic in the wake of headline-grabbing financial scandals such as the failure of British merchant bank Barings in 1995 after Singapore-based trader Nick Leeson ran up losses of almost $1.4 billion through unauthorised derivatives deals. Daiwa Bank was also hit by a scandal last year when it disclosed that a former bond trader at its New York branch incurred losses of $1.1 billion over an 11-year period.

However, the Commission currently thinks it is premature to adopt legally-binding legislation because other international authorities, such as the London-based International Accounting Standards Committee, are also discussing standards for derivatives accounting.

Monti will ultimately have to decide, possible before the end of the year, on whether to propose changing existing legislation on bank accounts or suggest a lighter instrument such as a recommendation.

On new payment systems, the Commission is planning to adopt at the end of the year a non-binding communication on traditional credit and debit cards as well as on electronic money such as smart cards -- cards with a built-in chip allowing the storage of useful information and even cash -- and payments over computer online networks.

The communication will try to address issues such as whether financial institutions should be the only ones allowed to issue cards or, for example, whether department stores could also have theirs; protection of consumers when shopping via computer online services like the Internet; the use of the same online services to launder money of criminal origin.
The EU executive is also expected to propose legally-binding rules to ensure people victim of car accidents in a foreign EU country are compensated.

Currently, under the Green Card system, if, for example, an insured Belgian driver is held responsible for an accident in Germany where he is visiting, a German victim of the accident will get compensated.
But if the victim in the same accident is the Belgian is likely that it will be both long and difficult to obtain redress.

The European insurance committee (CEA), which represents the industry, expects the Commission to propose that each insurance company should appoint an agent in all EU states, a solution accepted by the sector.
